claims.claim: Miracles still happen today, as they did in the Bible.
God still speaks to people through dreams and visions.

stances.summary: The Church still does what the apostles did. Christians drive out demons, heal the sick by laying on hands, and have even raised the dead, who lived among us for years.
stances.quote: Others still, heal the sick by laying their hands upon them, and they are made whole. Yea, moreover, as I have said, the dead even have been raised up, and remained among us for many years.
stances.translation: Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut, ANF vol. 1, 1885
stances.context: Written about 180 against Gnostic teachers whose wonders he calls magic. The same paragraph: "some do certainly and truly drive out devils" and "Others have foreknowledge of things to come: they see visions". He stresses the Church takes no money for these works. In 2.31.2 he again says the dead have been raised "frequently". Orthodox bishop; no change of mind.

stances.summary: Anyone can see it for themselves: Christians in Rome and everywhere cast out demons in the name of Jesus, where pagan exorcists and drugs had failed.
stances.quote: For numberless demoniacs throughout the whole world, and in your city, many of our Christian men exorcising them in the name of Jesus Christ, who was crucified under Pontius Pilate, have healed and do heal
stances.translation: Marcus Dods and George Reith, ANF vol. 1, 1885
stances.context: Addressed to the Roman Senate, about 150-160. He appeals to what the readers can observe "under your own observation". The claim is about exorcism, which is the kind of present-day wonder most Fathers cite. Orthodox; martyred about 165.

stances.summary: Christians are healing people right now, even men of high rank, and the emperor Severus himself was cured by a Christian and kept him at court.
stances.quote: How many men of rank (to say nothing of common people) have been delivered from devils, and healed of diseases!
stances.translation: S. Thelwall, ANF vol. 3, 1885
stances.context: An open letter of 212 to the proconsul of Africa, pleading against persecution. He names cases the governor could check: a clerk freed from an evil spirit, and Proculus Torpacion, who cured Septimius Severus "by anointing". Written in his Montanist period, but his earlier Apology (197), chapter 23, makes the same challenge: bring a possessed man before a Christian and watch the demon confess.

stances.summary: The great signs of the apostles have faded, but traces of the Spirit remain among Christians. They still drive out evil spirits, cure many, and foresee some events.
stances.quote: And there are still preserved among Christians traces of that Holy Spirit which appeared in the form of a dove. They expel evil spirits, and perform many cures, and foresee certain events, according to the will of the Logos.
stances.translation: Frederick Crombie, ANF vol. 4, 1885
stances.context: Written about 248. The qualification is his own: in book 7, chapter 8 (https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/04167.htm) he writes that the Spirit's signs were many at the beginning, "but since that time these signs have diminished, although there are still traces of His presence in a few who have had their souls purified by the Gospel". So: fewer than in the Bible, but not gone. Origen was condemned posthumously (553) on other matters.

stances.summary: God still acts visibly in the Church. He tells what he himself saw: a baby who had been fed pagan sacrifice could not keep down the Eucharist.
stances.quote: In a profane body and mouth the Eucharist could not remain; the draught sanctified in the blood of the Lord burst forth from the polluted stomach. So great is the Lord's power, so great is His majesty.
stances.translation: Robert Ernest Wallis, ANF vol. 5, 1886
stances.context: Written in 251 after the Decian persecution. The chapter opens "Learn what occurred when I myself was present and a witness". Chapter 26 adds a woman deterred by fire rising from the box holding the Eucharist, and a man who found only a cinder in his hands. These are wonders of judgment rather than healing, told to warn those who lapsed. Orthodox bishop, martyred 258.

stances.summary: The Holy Spirit still equips the whole Church with prophets, tongues, powers and healings.
stances.quote: This is He who places prophets in the Church, instructs teachers, directs tongues, gives powers and healings, does wonderful works, often discrimination of spirits, affords powers of government, suggests counsels, and orders and arranges whatever other gifts there are of charismata
stances.translation: Robert Ernest Wallis, ANF vol. 5, 1886
stances.context: Written about 240-250, before his schism of 251 (he later led a rigorist rival church at Rome; mark as schismatic, not heretical on the Trinity). The passage moves from the apostles to the Church in general, in the present tense: "and thus make the Lord's Church everywhere, and in all, perfected and completed." A doctrinal statement, not a report of cases, so strength 1.

stances.summary: Just as Christ drove out demons, His followers still drive them out today, in His name and by the sign of the cross.
stances.quote: For as He Himself, when He was living among men, put to flight all the demons by His word, and restored to their former senses the minds of men which had been excited and maddened by their dreadful attacks; so now His followers, in the name of their Master, and by the sign of His passion, banish the same polluted spirits from men.
stances.translation: William Fletcher, ANF vol. 7, 1886
stances.context: Written about 305-311. He adds that pagan sacrifices fail and diviners fall silent when a Christian with the sign of the cross on his forehead stands by, which he says provoked persecution. The line draws the Bible-to-now parallel the quiz claim asks about.

stances.summary: Nobody should doubt that a man like Antony worked real wonders. Christ promised that faith would move mountains, and He keeps His word.
stances.quote: Such are the words of Antony, and we ought not to doubt whether such marvels were wrought by the hand of a man.
stances.translation: H. Ellershaw, NPNF 2nd series vol. 4, 1892
stances.context: Written about 357, soon after Antony died; Athanasius knew him. He goes on to quote Matthew 17:20 ("If you have faith as a grain of mustard seed..."), and chapter 84 adds: "Antony, at any rate, healed not by commanding, but by prayer and speaking the name of Christ." The Life is full of cures and exorcisms and was meant to be read as proof that the age of wonders had not ended. Orthodox bishop of Alexandria.

stances.summary: Signs still happen, but they are Christ's work, not ours. Never boast of casting out demons or healing. Rejoice that your name is in heaven.
stances.quote: For the working of signs is not ours but the Saviour's work: and so He said to His disciples: Rejoice not that the demons are subject to you, but that your names are written in the heavens
stances.translation: H. Ellershaw, NPNF 2nd series vol. 4, 1892
stances.work: Life of Antony (by Athanasius), Antony's sermon to the monks
stances.context: Words put in Antony's mouth by Athanasius, who knew him. The same chapter: "it is not fitting to boast at the casting forth of the demons, nor to be uplifted by the healing of diseases". Antony takes it for granted that monks cast out demons and heal; his point is humility. The Life says he himself healed many (chapters 56-58, 84).

stances.summary: A blind man in Milan was healed when he touched the cloth over the martyrs' relics. It is just like the blind man in the Gospel, and those who deny it cannot deny the fact.
stances.quote: They deny that the blind man received sight, but he denies not that he is healed. He says: I who could not see now see. He says: I ceased to be blind, and proves it by the fact. They deny the benefit, who are unable to deny the fact.
stances.translation: H. de Romestin, E. de Romestin and H.T.F. Duckworth, NPNF 2nd series vol. 10, 1896
stances.context: June 386, when Ambrose found the bodies of Gervasius and Protasius. The blind man was Severus, a butcher known in the city. The next section asks: "Is not this like that which we read in the Gospel?" The "they" who denied the miracle were the Arian party at court (see notes). Augustine, then in Milan, cites the same healing in Confessions 9.7 and City of God 22.8.

stances.summary: The monk Hilarion worked more miracles than can be told, but his humility is more wonderful than his miracles.
stances.quote: Some may wonder at the miracles he worked, or his incredible fasting, knowledge, and humility. Nothing so astonishes me as his power to tread under foot honour and glory.
stances.translation: W.H. Fremantle, G. Lewis and W.G. Martley, NPNF 2nd series vol. 6, 1893
stances.context: Written about 390 about a monk who died in 371. Section 24: "Time would fail me if I wished to relate all the miracles which were wrought by him." Jerome treats recent miracles as fact while ranking virtue above them. He did not know Hilarion personally; he relied on Epiphanius and others.

stances.summary: Miracles are not done now, and that is for our good. The more overwhelming the proof, the less room for faith, and faith is what God rewards.
stances.quote: It follows that by how much the more evident and overpowering the course of events, by so much is the part of faith abridged. For this reason miracles are not done now.
stances.translation: Talbot W. Chambers, NPNF 1st series vol. 12, 1889
stances.context: Preached at Antioch, about 392. He cites John 20:29, "Blessed are they who have not seen, and yet have believed", and adds that if the Church lived as in Acts 4 "we should convert the whole world, even without miracles". Homily 29 (https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/220129.htm) says the gifts of 1 Corinthians 12 were "such as then used to occur but now no longer take place". Qualification: he did not deny every wonder. In his Homily on St Babylas (https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1906.htm) he speaks of "the grace of the Holy Spirit, which pleads to all on behalf of the resurrection, by means of the wonders which it works" at a martyr's grave. So: no apostolic-style signs now, but God still honours the martyrs.

stances.original: Cum enim Ecclesia catholica per totum orbem diffusa atque fundata sit, nec miracula illa in nostra tempora durare permissa sunt, ne anima semper visibilia quaereret, et eorum consuetudine frigesceret genus humanum, quorum novitate flagravit
stances.summary: Early view: once the Church had spread through the world, God did not let those miracles continue, so that people would stop chasing visible things and not grow bored of wonders.
stances.quote: Now that the Catholic Church has been spread and founded through the whole world, those miracles were not allowed to last into our times, so that the soul would not always be seeking visible things, and the human race would not grow cold through getting used to the very things whose newness had set it on fire.
stances.translation: own rendering from the Latin (the English of J.H.S. Burleigh, 1953, is in copyright)
stances.context: Written about 390, soon after his conversion. HE LATER CORRECTED THIS. In the Retractations (about 427), book 1, chapter 13, section 7 (Latin at https://la.wikisource.org/wiki/Retractationum_libri_duo) he says the sentence is true of tongues at baptism and of healing by an apostle's shadow, but adds, in my rendering: "But what I said must not be taken to mean that no miracles are to be believed to happen now in the name of Christ. For I myself, when I wrote that very book, already knew that a blind man had been given sight at the bodies of the martyrs in Milan... and so many such things happen even in these times that we can neither know them all nor count those we do know." Latin: "Sed non sic accipiendum est quod dixi, ut nunc in Christi nomine fieri miracula nulla credantur. Nam ego ipse, quando istum ipsum librum scripsi, ad Mediolanensium corpora martyrum in eadem civitate caecum illuminatum fuisse iam noveram et alia nonnulla, qualia tam multa etiam istis temporibus fiunt, ut nec omnia cognoscere nec ea quae cognoscimus, enumerare possimus." See his later stance below.

stances.summary: Late view: miracles are still done in Christ's name, through the sacraments and the prayers and relics of the saints. At Hippo alone almost seventy were written up in two years.
stances.quote: For even now miracles are wrought in the name of Christ, whether by His sacraments or by the prayers or relics of His saints; but they are not so brilliant and conspicuous as to cause them to be published with such glory as accompanied the former miracles.
stances.translation: Marcus Dods, NPNF 1st series vol. 2, 1887
stances.context: Written about 426-427, the change of mind from On True Religion (about 390). The chapter lists some two dozen cures and several raisings from the dead in North Africa after the relics of St Stephen arrived (424-425), and says of Hippo: "those which have been published amount to almost seventy at the hour at which I write". He began having written accounts read out in church because "the multitude should not remain ignorant of these things". He still grants they are less famous than the Bible's miracles, because the canon of Scripture is read everywhere and these are not.

stances.summary: The desert fathers did real healings, but no one should be judged holy by his miracles. Mastering your own lust or anger is a greater miracle than casting a demon out of someone else.
stances.quote: And in truth it is a greater miracle to root out from one's own flesh the incentives to wantonness than to cast out unclean spirits from the bodies of others
stances.translation: Edgar C.S. Gibson, NPNF 2nd series vol. 11, 1894
stances.context: Written about 426-429, voiced by Abba Nesteros. Chapters 3-5 tell recent cures by Egyptian monks (Abraham the Simple restoring a mother's milk and a lame man's knee). Chapter 6: "men of corrupt minds, reprobate concerning the truth, both cast out devils and perform the greatest miracles". Cassian is later judged semi-Pelagian on grace by some in the West, but is a saint in the East.

stances.summary: Martin healed and cast out demons all his life, and he said his power to do so had been greater when he was a monk than after he became a bishop.
stances.quote: I have often noticed this, Sulpitius, that Martin was accustomed to say to you, that such an abundance of power was by no means granted him while he was a bishop, as he remembered to have possessed before he obtained that office.
stances.translation: Alexander Roberts, NPNF 2nd series vol. 11, 1894
stances.context: Martin's own saying, reported by his disciple Gallus to Sulpicius Severus, who knew Martin personally (Dialogues written about 404). Dialogue 3, chapter 13 (https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/35033.htm) adds that after taking communion with the bishops who had Priscillian executed, Martin "confessed to us with tears that he felt a diminution of his power". The Life of Martin (https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/3501.htm, chapter 7-8) tells of him raising the dead. In Dialogue 2 the speaker Gallus admits that "human infirmity doubted concerning the works of Martin".

stances.summary: His sister Macrina healed the sick, cast out demons and foretold the future. He leaves most of it out, because people judge what is possible by their own small experience.
stances.quote: Healings of diseases, and castings out of demons, and true predictions of the future.
stances.translation: W.K. Lowther Clarke, Life of St. Macrina, SPCK, 1916
stances.context: Written about 380, soon after Macrina's death, by her brother. The quoted phrase lists the wonders he chose to omit. Just before: "For most men judge what is credible in the way of a tale by the measure of their own experience." He adds that spiritual gifts are given "according to the proportion of faith". He also records a soldier's account of Macrina curing his daughter's eye: "What is there surprising in the blind recovering their sight by the hand of God, when now His handmaiden, accomplishing those cures by faith in Him, has worked a thing not much inferior to those miracles?" Macrina herself, as a girl, refused a doctor for a tumour and was healed after her mother made the sign of the cross (same Life). Orthodox.

stances.summary: His own father was worthy of the miracles by which God confirms true religion, and he tells of healings in his family.
stances.quote: Such being his birth, such his exercise of the priestly office, such the reputation which he won at the hands of all, what wonder if he was thought worthy of the miracles by which God establishes true religion?
stances.translation: Charles Gordon Browne and James Edward Swallow, NPNF 2nd series vol. 7, 1894
stances.work: Oration 18, funeral oration on his father
stances.context: Preached in 374. Sections 28-29 describe his father's recovery from a deadly fever on Easter night; section 30 opens "The same miracle occurred in the case of my mother", healed after a dream. He treats such things as ordinary signs of God's favour in his own day. Orthodox.

stances.original: Nunquidnam, fratres mei, quia ista signa non facitis, minime creditis? Sed haec necessaria in exordio Ecclesiae fuerunt. Ut enim fides cresceret, miraculis fuerat nutrienda, quia et nos cum arbusta plantamus, tandiu eis aquam infundimus, quousque ea in terra jam convaluisse videamus; et si semel radicem fixerint, in rigando cessamus.
stances.summary: The outward signs Jesus promised were needed at the Church's beginning, like water for a young tree; now the Church does spiritually what the apostles did bodily. Yet he also collected many miracles of holy men of his own day.
stances.quote: Surely, my brothers, you do not fail to believe just because you do not do these signs? These things were needed at the beginning of the Church. For faith had to be fed with miracles so that it would grow. When we plant young trees, we pour water on them until we see they have taken hold in the ground; once they have put down roots, we stop watering.
stances.translation: own rendering from the Latin (no English before 1929 found)
stances.context: Preached about 591 on the Ascension. He goes on: the Church "daily does spiritually what it then did bodily through the apostles": exorcism by priests, new tongues in those who praise God, etc. BUT two years later his Dialogues (593-594) are a book of recent Italian miracles. When his deacon Peter says he knows of no one in Italy who worked miracles, Gregory answers that if he told only what he had from credible witnesses, "I should sooner in mine opinion lack day to talk in, than matter to speak of" (Dialogues book 1, prologue, 1608/1911 English at https://www.tertullian.org/fathers/gregory_01_dialogues_book1.htm). He also writes there that Libertinus's "patience ... did far excel all his signs and miracles". So: signs are not the norm or the proof, but God still works them through saints.

stances.original: siquidem et Nabuchodonosor diuinitus somniat et maior paene uis hominum ex uisionibus deum discunt.
stances.summary: God promised to pour out His Spirit so that people would see visions and dream dreams. Most people in fact come to know God through dreams, though demons send dreams too.
stances.quote: It was, indeed by an inspiration from God that Nebuchadnezzar dreamt his dreams; and almost the greater part of mankind get their knowledge of God from dreams.
stances.translation: Peter Holmes, ANF vol. 3, 1885
stances.context: Written about 210-213, in his Montanist period (mark as heterodox then). He sorts dreams: "inflicted on us mainly by demons", some from God (citing Joel: "His servants and His handmaids should see visions"), some from the soul, some from nature. The famous line is often quoted as "the majority of men learn God from dreams". Latin from https://www.tertullian.org/latin/de_anima.htm. In chapter 9 he describes a woman in his congregation who regularly received visions during worship.

stances.summary: In prison she knew she could ask the Lord for a vision and receive one. She asked, and was shown a ladder to heaven that told her she would die a martyr.
stances.quote: And I, who knew that I was privileged to converse with the Lord, whose kindnesses I had found to be so great, boldly promised him, and said, 'Tomorrow I will tell you.' And I asked, and this was what was shown me.
stances.translation: R.E. Wallis, ANF vol. 3, 1885
stances.work: The Passion of Perpetua and Felicity
stances.context: Carthage, 203. This part is Perpetua's own account. She records four visions (the ladder and dragon, her dead brother Dinocrates twice, the fight with the Egyptian); her fellow martyr Saturus records another. Some link the text to Montanist circles because of its stress on new visions, but the Church has always honoured her as orthodox.

stances.person: Editor of the Passion of Perpetua (anonymous, c. 203)
stances.summary: The visions of our own day are promised by God just as the prophecies were, and should be written down and read in church, so no one thinks grace belonged only to the ancients.
stances.quote: And thus we — who both acknowledge and reverence, even as we do the prophecies, modern visions as equally promised to us
stances.translation: R.E. Wallis, ANF vol. 3, 1885
stances.work: The Passion of Perpetua and Felicity
stances.context: The unnamed editor who framed Perpetua's diary (sometimes guessed, without proof, to be Tertullian). He cites Joel 2:28 ("your young men shall see visions, and your old men shall dream dreams") and writes so "that no weakness or despondency of faith may suppose that the divine grace abode only among the ancients". Leans Montanist in tone.

stances.summary: God guides the Church by visions at night and by children seeing in ecstasy by day. People who laugh at dreams are the same people who will not obey their bishop.
stances.quote: Although I know that to some men dreams seem ridiculous and visions foolish, yet assuredly it is to such as would rather believe in opposition to the priest, than believe the priest.
stances.translation: Robert Ernest Wallis, ANF vol. 5, 1886
stances.location: Letter 68 in ANF numbering (66 in modern editions), to Florentius Puppianus, section 10
stances.context: About 254. Just before, he says God "condescended to show and to reveal" a warning to him. He compares himself to Joseph mocked as "this dreamer". In Letter 9 (ANF; 16 in modern editions, https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/050609.htm) he writes: "besides the visions of the night, by day also, the innocent age of boys is among us filled with the Holy Spirit, seeing in an ecstasy with their eyes". His deacon Pontius (Life of Cyprian, 12) says Cyprian foresaw his own martyrdom in a vision. Orthodox bishop, martyred 258.

stances.summary: Many people have been turned to Christ against their will by a vision by day or a dream by night. He has seen such cases himself.
stances.quote: many have been converted to Christianity as if against their will, some sort of spirit having suddenly transformed their minds from a hatred of the doctrine to a readiness to die in its defense, and having appeared to them either in a waking vision or a dream of the night.
stances.translation: Frederick Crombie, ANF vol. 4, 1885
stances.context: About 248. He continues: "Many such instances have we known", which he will not write down because unbelievers would mock them, and calls God to witness he is not lying. Posthumously condemned (553) on other doctrines.

stances.summary: Some believers in his day have foreknowledge, see visions, and speak prophecies.
stances.quote: Others have foreknowledge of things to come: they see visions, and utter prophetic expressions.
stances.translation: Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut, ANF vol. 1, 1885
stances.context: About 180, in a list of gifts the Church still exercises. In 5.6.1 (https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/0103506.htm) he writes "we do also hear many brethren in the Church, who possess prophetic gifts". About visions and prophecy in general, not dreams in particular.

stances.summary: The prophetic gifts that once belonged to Israel have passed to the Church and are still present.
stances.quote: For the prophetical gifts remain with us, even to the present time.
stances.translation: Marcus Dods and George Reith, ANF vol. 1, 1885
stances.context: About 155-160. Prophecy rather than dreams as such. He immediately warns that, as in Israel, there are "many false teachers among us". In chapter 39 (https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/01283.htm) he lists gifts believers receive: "another of healing, another of foreknowledge".

stances.summary: Demons send apparitions, but true visions of holy ones also come. You can tell them apart: a vision from God comes quietly and leaves joy and courage; a demonic one brings noise and fear.
stances.quote: The vision of the holy ones is not fraught with distraction: For they will not strive, nor cry, nor shall any one hear their voice. But it comes so quietly and gently that immediately joy, gladness and courage arise in the soul.
stances.translation: H. Ellershaw, NPNF 2nd series vol. 4, 1892
stances.work: Life of Antony (by Athanasius), Antony's sermon to the monks
stances.context: Antony's words as given by Athanasius, who knew him (Life written about 357). Most of the sermon (chapters 21-43) warns that demons take many shapes and "wish to tell the future". Antony himself had visions: in chapter 82 he foresaw the Arian seizure of the churches as mules kicking the altar, two years before it happened.

stances.summary: His father was converted partly by reasoning and partly by a dream, the kind God often gives to a soul worthy of salvation.
stances.quote: For the salvation of my father there was a concurrence of the gradual conviction of his reason, and the vision of dreams which God often bestows upon a soul worthy of salvation.
stances.translation: Charles Gordon Browne and James Edward Swallow, NPNF 2nd series vol. 7, 1894
stances.work: Oration 18, funeral oration on his father
stances.context: Preached in 374. In the dream his father found himself singing Psalm 122, "I was glad when they said to me, we will go into the house of the Lord", and was baptized soon after (325). Section 30 tells how his sick mother dreamed Gregory fed her blessed loaves: "The nocturnal vision was a real action." Orthodox.

stances.summary: God can and does teach through dreams: a doubting doctor was convinced of life after death by a dream. But many dreams are our own, and the dead who appear in dreams are not really the dead.
stances.quote: This believer says that by this means all doubts as to this matter were removed from him. By whom was he taught this but by the merciful, providential care of God?
stances.translation: J.G. Cunningham, NPNF 1st series vol. 1, 1887
stances.context: About 415. Gennadius, a Carthage physician who doubted the afterlife, twice dreamed of a youth who showed him he could see while his bodily eyes were shut. Augustine adds that anyone is free to believe or disbelieve the story. Qualifications: in On the Care of the Dead (about 421), 16 (https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1316.htm), he says the dead seen in dreams are "angelic operations through dispensation of the providence of God", which may instruct or deceive. In Confessions 6.13 he reports his mother's claim to tell God's revelations from her own dreams (see Monica).

stances.summary: God sometimes showed her things in dreams, and she could tell those apart from ordinary dreams by a kind of taste she could not put into words.
stances.quote: For she could, she declared, through some feeling which she could not express in words, discern the difference between Your revelations and the dreams of her own spirit.
stances.translation: J.G. Pilkington, NPNF 1st series vol. 1, 1887
stances.context: Her words as reported by her son (written about 397-400). When she prayed for a vision about his marriage, she saw only "vain and fantastic things" and told them to him "not with her usual confidence when You had shown her anything". Book 3, chapter 11 tells her earlier dream of standing on a wooden rule, which she took as God's promise of his conversion. Not in the quiz pool; recorded as an early Christian voice.

stances.summary: He saw Christ in a dream wearing the half cloak he had given a beggar, and angels spoke with him. But he tested visions: a Christ in royal purple without the wounds was the devil.
stances.quote: The Lord Jesus did not predict that he would come clothed in purple, and with a glittering crown upon his head. I will not believe that Christ has come, unless he appears with that appearance and form in which he suffered, and openly displaying the marks of his wounds upon the cross.
stances.translation: Alexander Roberts, NPNF 2nd series vol. 11, 1894
stances.context: Martin's own words, which Sulpicius says he had "from the lips of Martin himself" (Life written about 396, while Martin was alive). Chapter 3 tells Martin's dream of Christ in the cloak; Dialogue 2, chapter 13 says "angels often appeared and spoke familiarly with Martin". So he believed God speaks this way, and judged each vision by the Gospel. Orthodox.

stances.summary: When he prayed for direction, a voice from God answered him, twice, and he obeyed it.
stances.quote: he prayed to God, and said, “O Lord, direct me how to live”; and a voice came to him, saying, “Arsenius, flee from men, and thou shalt live.”
stances.translation: E. A. Wallis Budge, The Paradise or Garden of the Holy Fathers, vol. 2 (from the Syriac of Anan-Isho), 1907
stances.context: Arsenius left the imperial court about 394 for the Egyptian desert. The second saying repeats it: "Arsenius, flee, keep silence, and lead a life of silent contemplation". A voice in prayer rather than a dream. The same sayings appear in the Greek alphabetical collection (Arsenius 1-2).

stances.summary: Early view: he was dragged in a vision before Christ's judgment seat and beaten for loving Cicero more than Scripture. It was no idle dream: he woke with bruises and changed his reading.
stances.quote: And that this was no sleep nor idle dream, such as those by which we are often mocked, I call to witness the tribunal before which I lay, and the terrible judgment which I feared.
stances.translation: W.H. Fremantle, G. Lewis and W.G. Martley, NPNF 2nd series vol. 6, 1893
stances.context: Written in 384 about a fever-vision of about 375. The Judge said: "You are a follower of Cicero and not of Christ." He continues: "my shoulders were black and blue, that I felt the bruises long after I awoke". HE LATER PLAYED THIS DOWN: see his stance from about 401-402 below.

stances.summary: Later view: a promise made in a dream binds no one. The prophets say not to believe dreams; he has dreamed he was dead and could fly.
stances.quote: Still, when a man makes a dream into a crime, I can quote to him the words of the Prophets, who say that we are not to believe dreams; for even to dream of adultery does not condemn us to hell, and to dream of the crown of martyrdom does not raise us to heaven.
stances.translation: W.H. Fremantle, NPNF 2nd series vol. 3, 1892
stances.context: About 401-402. Rufinus had accused him of perjury for still quoting pagan authors after swearing in the vision of Letter 22 never to read them. Jerome now calls it "a mere dream" and says "a promise given in a dream must not be pressed". This is a self-defence in a bitter quarrel, so it may say more about the quarrel than about a settled theology of dreams, but it is his later word.

stances.summary: Most dreams come from the body and the day's memories. Dreams sent by God, as to Joseph and Daniel, are exceptions and should not be lumped with ordinary dreams. Yet he read his own dream before Macrina's death as a sign.
stances.quote: Thus we must reckon these cases as exceptional, and not class them with common dreams.
stances.translation: H.A. Wilson, NPNF 2nd series vol. 5, 1893
stances.context: Written 379. The chapter gives a physical account of dreams, then excepts the God-given dreams of Scripture. But in the Life of Macrina (1916 English at https://www.tertullian.org/fathers/gregory_macrina_1_life.htm) he tells how, a day from her convent, "a vision appeared to me in a dream", martyrs' relics blazing with light, three times in one night, and "I watched carefully so as to judge the vision by events"; she was dying. He also says their mother was told Macrina's secret name, Thecla, in a dream. Orthodox.

stances.summary: Dreams come from six sources: a full or empty stomach, the devil, our thoughts, or God. Because you cannot easily tell which, be all the slower to believe them. Holy people can taste the difference.
stances.quote: But seeing dreams do grow from such divers roots, with so much the more difficulty ought we to believe them: because it doth not easily appear unto us, from what cause they do proceed.
stances.translation: P.W. (1608), revised by Edmund G. Gardner, 1911
stances.location: book 4, chapter 48 in this edition (4.50 in modern editions)
stances.context: Written 593-594. The six kinds: "too much fulness or emptiness of the stomach", illusion, thought and illusion, revelation, thought and revelation. He cites Joseph and the angel who warned Mary's spouse as real revelation, and Sirach "Dreams have made many to err" as the warning. He continues: "Holy men, indeed, by a certain inward spiritual taste, do discern betwixt illusions and true revelations". The next chapter tells of a man promised long life in a dream who died soon after. Pope; orthodox.

stances.summary: Revelations and dreams have ruined great ascetics. Without discernment and humble counsel, a monk will take the devil for an angel.
stances.quote: at last was so deceived by revelations and dreams that came from the devil that after so many labours and good deeds, in which he had surpassed all those who dwelt in the same parts, he actually relapsed miserably into Judaism and circumcision of the flesh.
stances.translation: Edgar C.S. Gibson, NPNF 2nd series vol. 11, 1894
stances.context: Written about 426, voiced by Abba Moses on discretion. Chapter 5: the old man Heron, after fifty years in the desert, "received with the utmost reverence an angel of Satan as an angel of light" and threw himself down a well. Chapter 7: a monk who "for a long while received a devil in the brightness of an angelic form" and nearly sacrificed his son like Abraham. The devil first reveals true things to win trust. Cassian does not deny that God gives revelations; his point is that they must never be trusted over discretion and the elders.

stances.summary: If you see visions or hear rumours, do not pass them on to your neighbour. Keeping quiet is the victory.
stances.quote: If thou seest visions and hearest rumours, repeat them not to thy neighbour, for this is victory of the war.
stances.translation: E. A. Wallis Budge, The Paradise or Garden of the Holy Fathers, vol. 2 (from the Syriac of Anan-Isho), 1907
stances.context: Poemen was a leading Egyptian elder of the fifth century. The saying takes visions as something that happens to monks, and counsels silence about them rather than trust or display. It does not say whether they come from God. A weak signal for the quiz.

stances.person: Desert elder (anonymous, Sayings of the Fathers)
stances.summary: When a figure appeared saying "I am Christ", the old man mocked it: he did not want to see Christ in this life. If an angel appears, say you are not worthy.
stances.quote: And the old man answered and said unto him, “I do not desire to see Christ here”; and when Satan heard these things he departed from him and was no more seen.
stances.translation: E. A. Wallis Budge, The Paradise or Garden of the Holy Fathers, vol. 2 (from the Syriac of Anan-Isho), 1907
stances.location: Book 2, Questions and Answers on the Rule of Life of the Holy Men, saying 36
stances.context: Egyptian desert, fourth-fifth century; the collection is near-contemporary. Saying 28 on the same page: Satan appears as Gabriel; the old man says "Hast thou not been sent unto another? for I am a sinner", and teaches: "If in very truth an angel appeareth unto thee, say... I am not worthy." The desert did not deny true visions (the same collection mentions elders "who used to see visions"); its rule was to refuse and distrust them.

stances.original: Ὁ τοίνυν ὀνείροις πιστεύων ὅμοιός ἐστι τῷ τὴν σκιὰν ἑαυτοῦ κατατρέχοντι, καὶ ταύτην κατέχειν δοκιμάζοντι. ... Ὁ ἐνυπνίοις πεισθεὶς εἰς ἅπαν ἀδόκιμος. Ὁ δὲ πᾶσιν ἀπιστῶν, φιλόσοφος οὗτος·
stances.summary: Trusting dreams is like chasing your own shadow. Demons pose as prophets in sleep. The wise man distrusts every dream, except those that warn him of judgment.
stances.quote: So whoever puts faith in dreams is like a man chasing his own shadow and trying to catch hold of it. ... Whoever is won over by dreams is wholly untested; but whoever distrusts them all is a true lover of wisdom.
stances.translation: own rendering from the Greek (the English of Lazarus Moore, 1959, and later versions are in copyright)
stances.location: Step 3 (on exile), closing section on dreams
stances.context: Sinai, about 600-650. Between the two lines: "Demons of vainglory are prophets in sleep", guessing the future and foretelling it so that we think ourselves near the gift of foreknowledge. After them: believe only dreams that announce punishment and judgment to you, and if even those bring despair, they too are from demons. The shadow image echoes Sirach 34:2. Orthodox saint. The Greek text on Wikisource has footnote numbers inside nearby sentences; the quoted Greek avoids them.

stances.summary: Do not long to see angels, powers or Christ with your senses in prayer. You will be deceived and end up worshipping demons.
stances.quote: Do not long to see angels or powers or Christ with your bodily senses, or you may go completely out of your mind, welcoming a wolf in place of the shepherd and bowing down to demons who are your enemies.
stances.translation: own rendering, made from a modern Greek version of the text (the original Greek was not loaded; English of Palmer, Sherrard and Ware, 1979, and of Sinkewicz, 2003, are in copyright)
stances.work: On Prayer (153 chapters; in the Philokalia under the name of Nilus)
stances.context: Late fourth century. Chapter 114: do not seek any form or shape at the time of prayer. Chapter 116: the start of the mind's delusion is vainglory, which makes it try to picture the divine in shapes. The context is prayer, not sleep, so this is about visions sought in prayer rather than dreams. Scholars attribute the work to Evagrius; the Philokalia prints it as by Nilus. Evagrius was condemned with Origenist teachings in 553; mark heterodox. STATUS: the page read is a modern Greek translation ("Μην ποθείς να ιδείς αγγέλους ή δυνάμεις ή το Χριστό αισθητά..."), so check against the Greek (PG 79, 1192-3, or the Philokalia) before any wording is shown to readers.

stances.original: Ταῦτα συμβαίνει τοῖς ἰδιώταις καὶ ἐλαφροῖς ἀνθρώποις, οἳ ταῖς μὲν γραφαῖς ἀκριβῶς οὐ προσέχουσιν, ταῖς δὲ ἀνθρωπίναις παραδόσεσιν καὶ ταῖς ἑαυτῶν πλάναις καὶ τοῖς ἑαυτῶν ἐνυπνίοις καὶ μυθολογίαις καὶ λόγοις γραώδεσι μᾶλλον πείθονται.
stances.summary: A bishop in Pontus trusted his own dreams over Scripture, predicted the Judgment within a year, and ruined his flock. Such things happen to people who prefer their own dreams to the Scriptures.
stances.quote: These things happen to untaught and light-minded people, who do not pay close attention to the Scriptures, but would rather trust human traditions, their own errors, their own dreams, fables and old wives' tales.
stances.translation: own rendering from the Greek (the English of T.C. Schmidt, 2010, is in copyright)
stances.context: About 204. Chapter 19: a pious and humble church leader in Pontus "did not attend carefully to the Scriptures, but trusted rather the visions which he himself saw". After one, two, three dreams came true he began to prophesy; he announced the Judgment in a year; people abandoned fields and sold property; when nothing happened "the Scriptures were shown to be true" and those who sold up ended as beggars. Chapter 18 tells a similar story of a Syrian bishop who led his people into the desert to meet Christ. Greek read in Bonwetsch, Hippolytus Werke 1 (GCS, 1897), from a raw OCR text; the OCR is garbled in places (e.g. "γραώδεσι" appears as "yoamdecı"), so the Greek above is normalised. Hippolytus was a rival bishop at Rome for a time, later reconciled and martyred (235).

splits_fathers: Claim a: nearly every early Christian who speaks to it says wonders still happen, above all exorcisms and healings, and from the 380s cures at martyrs' relics. The real dissent is narrower: that the great public signs of the apostles (tongues at baptism, healing by a shadow) have ceased. Chrysostom says it bluntly ("miracles are not done now") and gives a reason (so that faith keeps its reward), yet credits wonders at martyrs' graves. Augustine said miracles had not been allowed to continue (about 390) and then reversed himself with a list of about seventy cures at Hippo (about 426). Gregory the Great calls signs the water a young tree needs, then fills a book with Italian miracles. Origen says the signs have "diminished" to "traces". So a real two-sided question exists only if the statement pits apostolic-scale miracles against "God still does wonders"; framed as "miracles still happen at all", it is one-sided among the Fathers. Claim b: this one is genuinely split. The second- and third-century voices (Irenaeus, Justin, Tertullian, Perpetua and her editor, Cyprian, Origen) and the Cappadocians' family stories (Gregory of Nazianzus, Gregory of Nyssa's own dream) treat dreams and visions as a live way God speaks. From the desert onward the dominant note is distrust: Hippolytus's bishop of Pontus, Cassian's ruined monks, the desert elders who refuse visions of Christ and angels, Evagrius against seeking visions in prayer, Gregory the Great's six causes and "be slow to believe", and John Climacus: whoever trusts dreams chases his own shadow. Jerome is on both sides at different times. Almost no one denies that God can send a dream; the split is over whether you should trust one.
splits_people_today: Claim a: Pentecostal and charismatic Christians (a very large share of Christians worldwide), Catholics and Orthodox (who canonise saints on attested miracles and venerate relics) mostly agree. Many Protestants in the Reformed and dispensational traditions hold that miraculous gifts ceased with the apostles (cessationism) while God still answers prayer through ordinary means, so they would disagree or hedge. Secular people mostly disagree; many "spiritual but not religious" people agree loosely. US surveys (Pew) have found a clear majority of Americans say miracles still occur today, so the statement leans agree in the general US public but splits sharply by tradition. Claim b: stronger split. Charismatics, many Christians in the Global South, and many Muslims agree; many evangelicals are wary (Scripture is sufficient; test the spirits); Catholics and Orthodox allow private revelation but teach caution and obedience to the Church; most secular people think dreams are brain activity. This claim will divide a Christian audience more evenly than claim a. A good quiz item may need to separate "God can speak through a dream" (most Christians agree) from "I would act on a dream I believed came from God" (the Fathers' real split).

misattributions.line: Miracles are not contrary to nature, but only contrary to what we know about nature.
misattributions.truth: A loose modern paraphrase of City of God 21.8. The NPNF wording is "A portent, therefore, happens not contrary to nature, but contrary to what we know as nature" (https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/120121.htm). The sense is genuine, but it is about portents in general, and the popular form is not his wording.

misattributions.line: Augustine taught that miracles ceased with the apostles.
misattributions.truth: Only his early view (On True Religion 25.47, about 390). He corrected it himself in the Retractations 1.13.7 and City of God 22.8. Quoting the early line alone misrepresents him.

He did say "miracles are not done now" (Homily 6 on 1 Corinthians) and that the gifts of 1 Corinthians 12 no longer happen (Homily 29), but he also praised the wonders the Spirit works at martyrs' graves (Homily on St Babylas). He is not a clean example for either side.

misattributions.line: "He who believes in dreams is like a man who chases the wind" as a saying of John Climacus.
misattributions.truth: Climacus (Ladder, Step 3) says one who trusts dreams chases his own shadow; the "wind" half is from Sirach 34:2 ("Whoso regardeth dreams is like him that catcheth at a shadow, and followeth after the wind"), which he is echoing. The English that circulates online (Lazarus Moore, 1959) is in copyright.

misattributions.line: "The majority of men learn God from dreams."
misattributions.truth: Genuine in substance (On the Soul 47: "maior paene uis hominum ex uisionibus deum discunt"), but "almost" is dropped in the popular form, and he wrote it in his Montanist period in a chapter that says most dreams come from demons.

notes: Voices worth knowing that are not in the stances: (1) Florentius Puppianus, a Carthaginian Christian who mocked Cyprian's visions (Cyprian, Letter 68/66); his own words do not survive, only Cyprian's reply. (2) The Arian party at Milan in 386 denied the healing of the blind man Severus (Ambrose, Letter 22); again known only from their opponent. (3) In Sulpicius Severus's Dialogue 2 the speaker admits that "human infirmity doubted concerning the works of Martin". These are real early disbelievers but cannot be quoted in their own voice. Leads not pursued, to save effort: Pontius, Life of Cyprian 12 (Cyprian's vision of his martyrdom); Theodoret, Religious History (Syrian monks' miracles); Diadochus of Photice, On Spiritual Knowledge 36-38 (distrust of dreams); Isaac the Syrian (Wensinck's English of 1923 is public domain in the US and may have lines on seeking visions); Basil and Ephrem not checked. For the quiz writer: claim a as worded will get "agree" from almost every Father, so the farthest-Father logic needs a sharper item, e.g. "The miracles in the Bible were for then; God does not work that way now" (Chrysostom, early Augustine, Gregory's Homily 29 on one side; Irenaeus, Ambrose, late Augustine, Martin on the other). Claim b works better if it asks about trusting a dream, not whether God can send one: Tertullian, Perpetua, Cyprian, Origen, Gregory of Nazianzus on one side; Climacus, the desert elders, Hippolytus, Cassian, Gregory the Great, later Jerome on the other. Quotes marked own_rendering are my literal renderings; their "original" field holds the source-language wording, which was checked against the page at "url" except for Evagrius (secondary-only). All other quotes were matched character for character against the tag-stripped raw page.
